question: Whom does the worship of other deities (anya-devatā) really reach, and what does it yield?

sides.position: (As the Gītā describes them; no school is named) people moved by various desires resort to other deities, adopting their observances according to their own nature; they worship those forms with faith and obtain their desires from them.
arguments: their faith is real and steady (7.21–22)
they obtain their desires from the deities they propitiate (7.22)

sides.position: Kṛṣṇa: it is he who makes their faith unwavering and who ordains the fruits they obtain; the fruit of those of small understanding is finite — worshippers of the gods go to the gods, of the ancestors to the ancestors, of spirits to spirits, his devotees to him; they too worship him, but not according to rule (avidhi-pūrvakam); not recognising him in truth as the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices, they fall.
arguments: the Lord grants both the faith and the fruit (7.21–22)
he is the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices (9.24)
each goes to what he worships, and only the Lord's devotees come to him (7.23; 9.25)

notes: Both sides as the Gītā itself states them; the first side is known only from the Gītā's own report. Later lineages take up the question (cf. dsp:ekasarana-and-other-deities, obs:devatantara-bhajana). No reconciliation is attempted here (extraction layer).

question: Is the Lord who has come into manifestation in a human body only a manifest, human being?

sides.position: (As the Gītā reports it; no school is named) the unintelligent think of him as unmanifest come into manifestation (7.24); the deluded disregard him as one who has taken on a human body.

Kṛṣṇa: they do not know his supreme state (paraṃ bhāvam), imperishable and unsurpassed, as the great lord of beings; veiled by his yoga-māyā he is not manifest to all, and the deluded world does not recognise him as unborn and imperishable; he knows all beings past, present and future, but no one knows him.
arguments: his supreme state is imperishable and unsurpassed (7.24)
he is the great lord of beings (9.11)

notes: The commentators differ on exactly which view 7.24 rejects (that the Lord, formerly unmanifest, has now become manifest like an ordinary being; or that he is merely a manifest person). Bears on the coverage-map G question whether the ultimate is personal or impersonal; no reconciliation attempted here.
